newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: NATO invite seen long-term positive for investment.
newsitem.headline: NATO invite seen long-term positive for investment.

text.p: Invitations to join NATO should provide a long-term boost to investment in the Czech Republic, Hungary and Poland, though no immediate change in perception is to be expected, economists said on Wednesday.
At the same time, countries which missed out on the first wave of alliance enlargement may lose out in the competition for foreign cash, some analysts said.

"It will cost something but as a whole it must be a positive because it is a question of insurance," Petr Chvojka, chief economist of Ceskoslovenska Obchodny Banka, told Reuters at a central European economic summit in Salzburg.
However, several analysts said the NATO decision was so widely expected that no immediate change was to be expected.
The impact on the business environment in the region of NATO enlargement is a key theme of this year's Central and Eastern European Economic Summit.

Several East European leaders are flying to the meeting in Salzburg from Madrid, where the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation on Tuesday invited the Czech Republic, Poland and Hungary to join, probably in 1999.
Some economists have said that the prospects of NATO membership, and of early European Union membership, risk creating new economic divisions between the "haves" and "have nots" in Eastern Europe.
Speaking before the widely-expected NATO decision was announced, Hungarian Industry, Trade and Tourism Minister Szabolcs Fazakas said the invitation would give investors confidence in Hungary.
"It will be important for overseas investors like the United States and Japan and the Asian countries because a country which is a member of NATO is a country of total security," he said.
But some analysts said NATO's security guarantees would be less important than the perception that the three leading candidates had reached certain standards of economic and political development.

"It is a confirmation that political stability is at such a level, not only political stability but the whole process of going to Europe with its democratic traditions," said Pavel Sobisek, chief economist of Czech bank Zivnostenska Banka.
"These three countries have come the furthest on this path and that is probably more important for investors than the fact they would be shielded by NATO," he said by telephone from Prague.
The three states invited to join NATO also head most lists of countries likely to be the next new members of the European Union.
Sobisek said the NATO invitations could even be reflected in improved credit ratings, and cheaper access to funds, for the three chosen countries.
He said the fact Slovakia, the Czechs' former federation partner in Czechoslovakia until 1993, was not invited could have a negative impact on investment there.
"On the other hand, different kinds of investors will look at different indicators, not just this one," he said.

In Bucharest, analysts said the fact Romania missed out on NATO's first cut was unlikely to affect foreign capital inflows or markets as investors were more concerned with the country's progress in implementing reforms.
"Investors will not react to being kept out of NATO. They want to see stability of the national leu currency and macro-economic stability in general," a local broker said.
